title: The effect of low-dose aspirin on reversing frailty status in older prefrail and frail adults: a secondary analysis of the ASPREE randomised clinical trial

sections.abstract:
Chronic low-grade inflammation is hypothesised as a central driver of frailty. This study aims to evaluate whether low-dose aspirin can reverse frailty status among initially prefrail/frail older adults.

This was a post hoc subgroup analysis of the Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE), a randomised, placebo-controlled trial, involving community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years. The median (Interquartile range) follow-up was 4.7 (3.6–5.7) years. We included participants who were prefrail or frail at baseline, with frailty assessed using two validated measures: the Fried Frailty Phenotype (FFP) and the Deficit-Accumulation Frailty Index (FI). Frailty reversal was defined as a transition to a less severe state (from frail to prefrail/nonfrail, prefrail to nonfrail). The discrete-time survival model was used for outcome analysis; linear mixed-effects models compared longitudinal frailty trajectories between the treatment arms.

Among 6595 and 8766 participants included in the FFP and FI analyses, respectively, there was no significant difference in frailty status reversal between aspirin and placebo groups (FFP-HR: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.92–1.07; FI-HR: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.94–1.07). No significant difference was found in the change of FFP counts (β = 0.014, SE = 0.007, P = .06) and FI score (β = 0.0004, SE = 0.004, P = .37) between the aspirin and placebo groups over time, suggesting that aspirin neither reversed nor worsened frailty severity. Subgroup analyses revealed no effect modification by frailty risk factors such as age, sex, race and medical history.

Low-dose aspirin has no effect in reversing frailty among prefrail and frail individuals. The findings highlight the need to explore alternative anti-inflammatory medications for frailty management.
sections.introduction:
Frailty is a complex geriatric syndrome characterised by a progressive deterioration across multiple physiological systems, leading to reduced reserve capacity and heightened vulnerability to stressors [ 1 ]. Frail individuals commonly experience significant impairments in their abilities to perform everyday activities, leading directly to a reduced quality of life and increased dependency on others. Frail older adults have significantly increased risks of adverse events compared to robust peers, including higher incidences of falls, bone fractures, functional disability, dementia and other age-related morbidities [ 1 , 2 ].

Evidence increasingly supports the notion that frailty is not an irreversible condition [ 3 ]. Lifestyle interventions, particularly structured exercise, nutritional support and cognitive training, remain the most effective and evidence-based strategies [ 4 ]. However, the feasibility of such interventions is often limited in frail populations due to mobility impairments, lack of energy, cognitive decline or lack of access and support [ 5 ]. Several pharmacological drugs have shown early promise in preventing or improving frailty [ 6–8 ] Though encouraging, the evidence remains preliminary, and no drug has yet emerged as a standard of care for frailty.

Chronic low-grade inflammation has been hypothesised to play a central role in the pathophysiology of frailty [ 9 ]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-6, C-reactive protein (CRP) and tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-α are elevated in frail individuals and are implicated in sarcopenia, immune dysregulation and functional decline [ 10 , 11 ]. Aspirin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with well-established antiplatelet and anti-inflammatory properties, acting through irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, specifically COX-1 and COX-2 [ 12 , 13 ]. Beyond its established role in cardiovascular prevention, aspirin has also been explored in age-related conditions characterised by chronic low-grade inflammation [ 9 ]. A post hoc analysis of the ASPREE study by Espinoza et al. found that low-dose aspirin did not slow the progression to frailty in initially nonfrail individuals [ 14 ]. The absence of a measurable effect of aspirin in nonfrail individuals may reflect a mismatch between intervention and inflammatory status, rather than an overall lack of therapeutic potential. Prefrail and frail individuals representing a population with reduced physiological reserve and potentially greater exposure to chronic inflammatory stress may be more likely to benefit [ 15 ]. As no epidemiological study targeting pharmacological strategies has focused specifically on reversing frailty, using data from the ASPREE trial [ 16–18 ], this study aims to assess whether daily low-dose aspirin can promote frailty reversal among older adults initially prefrail or frail.
sections.methods:
This study was performed in accordance with the CONSORT guidelines. The eligibility criteria used in this study were directly adapted from the original ASPREE trial ( NCT01038583 ) [ 16–18 ]. Participants eligible for the ASPREE trial were community-dwelling adults aged ≥70 years from Australia and the USA (aged ≥65 years if US minorities). All participants provided written informed consent.

Trial screening of participants excluded anyone with a documented history of cardiovascular disease events; severe intercurrent illnesses predicted to cause death within 5 years; conditions known to significantly elevate the risk of bleeding; absolute contraindications to aspirin; severe uncontrolled hypertension (defined as systolic blood pressure ≥ 180 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥105 mmHg); dementia; or substantial functional impairment identified by severe difficulty or inability to independently perform any of the six Katz Activities of Daily Living during screening assessments [ 16 ]. In this present study, we further excluded participants who were classified as nonfrail at baseline, restricting our analytical cohort to only those individuals identified as either frail or prefrail, as defined by either of two definitions used, the Fried Frailty Phenotype (FFP) or the Deficit-Accumulation Frailty Index (FI).

Participants were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either daily administration of 100 mg aspirin tablet or a matching placebo. Randomisation was conducted using a web-based system, employing computer-generated permuted block randomisation with variable block sizes, stratified by site and age group (70–74, 75–79, ≥80 years). Participants, study researchers and staff were all blinded to the randomised treatment. The clinical trial commenced in March 2010 and concluded on 12 June 2017, providing a median (IQR) of 4.7 (3.6–5.7) years of follow-up.

The primary outcome was the time to frailty status reversal, defined as the first observed transition to a less frail category compared to baseline (e.g. from frail to prefrail or robust; or from prefrail to robust), regardless of any subsequent changes. Time was the duration between baseline and the first reversal. Measured at baseline and each annual follow-up visit, frailty outcomes were assessed using two established classifications from prior ASPREE post hoc analyses: the Adapted FFP and FI [ 19 , 20 ]. The definition and measurement approach are outlined in the Appendix 1 .

At baseline and subsequent annual follow-up in-person visits, data on demographic and lifestyle characteristics were collected through questionnaires. Data on medical history were obtained via participant self-report, physician correspondence and review of medical records. Physical assessments including body weight and waist circumference, 3 m gait speed and hand grip strength were measured by trained study staff during in-person visits. Concomitant medications were recorded through interviews, medication lists and communication with the participants’ family physicians. Ongoing monitoring of relevant clinical events was conducted through structured follow-up 6-month phone calls and annual in-person visits post-baseline.

All statistical analyses in this study were conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle. Translation of frailty status from baseline to follow-up was virtually shown by the Sankey plot. Because frailty was measured annually, for the main outcome analysis, a discrete-time survival model with one explanatory variable for randomised treatment was used to estimate the effect of low-dose aspirin versus placebo and accommodate interval-censored event times. A hazard ratio (HR) >1 indicated a higher likelihood (faster rate) of frailty status reversal in the aspirin group compared to placebo. As an ancillary analysis, we also compared the incidence rate of permanent progression (from prefrail to permanent frail) to frailty between the treatment arms among prefrail participants, with time defined as the first progression to frailty. The Cox proportional hazard model was used as an alternative model to account for the variation in the exact timing of annual visits for individuals relative to their anniversary from baseline.

To account for transition back and forth over time beyond just the first reversal, we further used linear mixed-effects models to compare the longitudinal trajectory of frailty status change between the aspirin and placebo groups. Frailty was assessed using either the FFP criteria count (0–5) or the continuous FI score (0–67). These models included fixed effects for treatment, time and their interaction, as well as random intercepts and slopes to take into account within-person and between-person variability.

To explore potential effect modification, subgroup analyses were conducted across major baseline frailty risk factors including high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP). The P -value for interaction was reported to evaluate potential effect modification. A sensitivity analysis was conducted by replacing the discrete-time survival model with Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard models to account for competing death risk.

All analyses were performed using Stata/SE 18. A two-sided P -value <.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results:
In the FFP analysis, 12 159 participants were excluded from the initial 19 114 due to being classed as nonfrail at baseline ( n = 10 936), had missing baseline frailty status values ( n = 484) and/or missing follow-up data on frailty status ( n = 1099), leaving 6595 participants in the final cohort. This comprises 6272 (95.1%) prefrail and 321 (4.9%) frail individuals at baseline ( Figure 1 ). In the FI analysis, 10 348 participants were excluded from the initial 19 114 due to being nonfrail at baseline ( n = 9793), missing baseline frailty status ( n = 4) and/or missing follow-up data on frailty status ( n = 551), leaving 8766 participants in the final cohort. This comprised 7357 (83.9%) prefrail and 1409 (16.1%) frail individuals at baseline ( Figure 1 ). The component distribution of FFP and the mean FI score at baseline are presented in Appendix 2 .

Flowchart for Fried Frailty Phenotype Analysis (left) and Frailty Index [ 30 ]. 6595 participants were included in the Fried frailty phenotype analysis and 8766 were included in the frailty index analysis.

In both the FFP and FI cohorts, demographic and clinical characteristics were well balanced between the aspirin and placebo groups. The mean age was 76.0 years (SD, 5.1) in the FFP cohort and 75.8 years (SD, 4.9) in the FI cohort. The proportion of female participants was slightly higher in the FI cohort (64.1% in the aspirin group and 63.7% in the placebo group) compared with the FFP cohort (58.1% and 57.3%, respectively). Most participants were White (88.6% in FFP; 90.5% in FI) ( Table 1 ).

Baseline characteristics in Fried Frailty Phenotype and Frailty Index cohorts by the randomisation arms

Ethnicity/Race ‘Other’ includes Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islanders, Native Americans, more than one race, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander and those who were not Hispanic and who did not state their ethnicity/race; diabetes is defined from self-report or fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dl (≥7 mmol/L) or on treatment for diabetes; and hypertension is defined as ‘on treatment’ for high BP or BP > 140/90 mmHg at study entry. Dyslipidaemia was defined as those taking cholesterol-lowering medications or serum cholesterol ≥212 mg/dl (≥5.5 mmol/L; Australia) and ≥240 mg/dl (≥6.2 mmol/L; U.S.) or LDL > 160 mg/dl (>4.1 mmol/L). CKD was defined as eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m 2 or albumin to creatinine ratio ≥ 3 mg/mmol; polypharmacy was defined as using five or more prescription medications. Previous regular aspirin use was self-reported regular use of aspirin immediately prior to first baseline visit with a 1-month washout prior to randomisation to study medication. Abbreviations: ACEi, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; ARB, angiotensin-receptor blocker; BMI, body mass index; CCB, calcium channel blocker; CKD, chronic kidney disease; NSAID, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; SD, standard deviation.

The transition of frailty status from baseline to follow-up is presented in Figure 2 . Among 6595 participants classified as prefrail or frail at baseline based on the FFP, 1383 participants experienced frailty reversal compared to baseline in the aspirin group (incidence rate [IR], 154.2 per 1000 person-years) and 1410 in the placebo group (IR, 154.4 per 1000 person-years). There was no statistically significant difference in frailty status reversal between the aspirin and placebo arms (HR = 1.00; 95% CI: 0.92–1.07; P = .92). A similar association was seen in the prefrail (HR = 1.00; 95% CI: 0.92–1.08; P = .90) and frail subgroups (HR = 0.96; 95% CI: 0.74–1.23; P = .75) ( Table 2 ). In the prefrail subgroup, 325 participants in the aspirin group and 328 in the placebo group have progressed to permanent frailty (IR, 28.6 and 28.5 per 1000 person-years, respectively). There is no difference between aspirin and placebo in progression to permanent frailty. (HR = 1.01, 95% CI, 0.86–1.18, P = .92).

Sankey plot for transition of frailty status. For Fried Frailty Phenotype (A), among 6274 participants who were prefrail at baseline, 2543 (41%) participants reversed to robust during the follow-up, while 2339 (37%) remained prefrail, and 1392 (22%) progressed to frail. Among 321 participants who were frail at baseline, 7 (2%) and 246 (77%) participants reversed to robust and pre-frail during follow-up, respectively, while 71 (22%) who were frail at baseline remained frail. For health deficit accumulation Frailty Index (B), among 7357 participants who were prefrail at baseline, 2871 (39%) participants reversed to robust during the follow-up, while 2304 (31%) remained pre-frail, and 2182 (30%) progressed to frail. Among 1409 participants who were frail at baseline, 28 (2%) and 609 (43%) participants reversed to robust and pre-frail during follow-up, respectively, while 772 (55%) who were frail at baseline remained frail.

Frailty status reversal between aspirin and placebo arms using discrete-time survival model to accommodate interval-censored event times

Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; FFP, Fried Frailty Index; FI, Frailty Index; HR, hazard ratio; IR, incidence rate per 1000 person-years.

Among 8766 participants categorised as prefrail or frail at baseline based on the FI, 1733 participants experienced reversal of frailty status in the aspirin group (IR, 138.6 per 1000 person-years) and 1775 in the placebo group (IR, 137.9 per 1000 person-years). Consistent with the results of FFP, there was no significant statistical difference in reversal of FI-defined frailty status between the aspirin and placebo groups in the overall cohort (HR = 1.00, 95% CI, 0.94–1.07; P = .98), and in the prefrail (HR = 0.99, 95% CI, 0.92–1.07; P = .86) and frail (HR = 1.02, 95% CI, 0.88–1.20; P = .78) subgroups, separately ( Table 2 ). In the prefrail subgroup, 650 participants in the aspirin group and 625 in the placebo group have progressed to permanent frailty (IR, 49.1 and 45.1 per 1000 person-years, respectively). No difference between aspirin and placebo was observed for progression to permanent frailty (HR = 1.09, 95% CI, 0.98–1.22, P = .11).

Repeating the analysis using the Cox model, a similar null effect was observed for aspirin ( Appendix 3 ). For the FFP, the HR was 1.00 (95% CI, 0.93–1.08; P = .99) in the overall cohort and was 1.00 (95% CI, 0.93–1.08; P = .99) in the prefrail subgroup and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.71–1.16; P = .42) in the frail subgroup. Similarly, in the FI cohort, no significant difference was detected between treatment groups in the overall cohort and subgroups (HR ranges between 1.00 and 1.03).

Appendixes 4 and 5 present the predicted mean FFP and FI scores separately in the aspirin and placebo groups from baseline through to the end of the trial period. Over the follow-up period, both frailty scores gradually increased in both groups. Analysis using a linear mixed-effects model found that FFP scores were increased by 0.011 units and FI scores were increased by 0.008 units annually across the whole cohort ( P = .029 and <.001, respectively). No significant difference was found in the change of FFP counts (β = 0.014, SE = 0.007, P = .06) and FI score (β = 0.0004, SE = 0.0004, P = .37) between the aspirin and placebo groups over time, suggesting that aspirin neither reversed nor worsened frailty severity ( Table 3 ).

Frailty trajectory over time in the aspirin and placebo groups

Abbreviations: FFP, Fried Frailty Phenotype; FI, Frailty Index; SE, standard error.

Subgroup analyses based on baseline characteristics did not reveal any significant interaction between selected baseline variables and aspirin treatment on FFP regression. ( Appendixes 6 and 7 ). In particular, the effect of aspirin on both the FFP and FI was not modified by baseline hs-CRP levels ( P for interaction = .17 and .30, respectively). Sensitivity analysis using Fine and Gray competing risk showed almost identical results as our main results ( Appendix 8 ).
sections.discussion:
This study demonstrated that daily low-dose aspirin did not significantly improve frailty status compared to placebo among older adults who were initially classified as prefrail or frail at enrolment into the ASPREE trial. These null findings were consistently supported across multiple analytic approaches and subgroups.

This study assessing the effect of aspirin on frailty reversal in the subset of ASPREE participants who were frail and prefrail at baseline complements our previous work evaluating the effect of aspirin on frailty prevention in the ASPREE participants who were robust at baseline [ 14 ]. In that earlier study, we found no statistically significant difference in the development of frailty between the aspirin and placebo groups (FFP HR: 1.04, 95% CI 0.96–1.13, P = .39; FI HR: 1.03, 95% CI 0.97–1.10, P = .29), which aligns with the findings of the current study. Similar consistency was also observed in the analysis tracking frailty score change over time. The continuity of null findings across both preventive and interventional contexts suggests a lack of clinical benefit from low-dose aspirin on managing frailty in older adults regardless of their baseline frailty status. This has provided important evidence further supporting the current clinical guidelines discouraging routine low-dose aspirin use in adults aged 70 years or older who were free of CVD [ 21 ].

Another study using extended data from the Physicians’ Health Study (PHS) clinical trial also investigated the effect of aspirin (325 mg every alternating day) on the development of frailty. The original randomised controlled trial commenced in 1982, evaluating the effect of aspirin and β-carotene for cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention among over 22 000 male physicians. The aspirin arm was terminated at the trial’s sixth year, and the cohort was continuously followed in a prospective observational manner, with self-reported aspirin use recorded annually [ 22 ]. A secondary analysis of the PHS cohort examined the relationship between long-term aspirin use and the prevalence of frailty at the completion of the extended observational phase (an average of 11.3 years of follow-up) in 12 101 male physicians aged ≥60 years [ 23 ]. Frailty was assessed using both the health-deficit accumulation FI and a modified Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (mSOF) phenotype. Participants who reported aspirin use over 60 days annually had 15% lower odds of frailty compared to those using aspirin 60 days or less (FI-defined OR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.76–0.96; P = .01). Similar trends were observed using the mSOF definition and across prefrail and frail categories (OR: 0.84; 95% CI: 0.72–0.99, P = .03). The favourable outcomes might be explained by a higher dose of aspirin used at the in-trial phase compared to ASPREE, raising questions about the dose-dependent relationship between aspirin use and frailty. In addition, PHS featured a markedly longer follow-up duration, over a decade, allowing potential anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin to accumulate over time and make tangible clinical benefits. However, these findings must be interpreted cautiously. In contrast to ASPREE where aspirin was randomised throughout the trial, the post-trial aspirin intake in the PHS study varied considerably in frequency, duration, and indication and was self-reported. Moreover, the observational nature of the PHS follow-up, combined with potential confounding by health behaviours and lack of adherence control, limits causal inference.

These observations raise an important consideration: it remains unclear whether the absence of effect in ASPREE reflects an insufficient dose and exposure duration to meaningfully influence frailty-related biology. Low-dose aspirin exerts its antithrombotic effect primarily through irreversible inhibition of platelet COX-1, leading to reduced thromboxane A2 production and subsequent suppression of platelet aggregation. Its efficacy in this regard is comparable to that of higher doses [ 24 ]. However, meaningful COX-2 inhibition, which is required to suppress the synthesis of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins like PGE2, typically necessitates higher systemic concentrations of aspirin. Since COX-2 is inducible and more transiently expressed during inflammatory states, especially in ageing tissues, low-dose aspirin may fall short in modulating this isoenzyme to a clinically relevant extent [ 25 , 26 ].

That said, the assumption that higher dosing ensures greater anti-inflammatory efficacy is not strongly supported by clinical data. A 6-week randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial by Hovens et al . [ 27 ] investigated the effects of both 100 and 300 mg aspirin in type 2 diabetic patients without cardiovascular disease. Both 100 and 300 mg doses yielded comparable reductions in inflammatory markers, with no statistically significant difference observed during the intervention. While the short duration of this trial may limit its applicability to chronic inflammatory states such as frailty, these findings suggest that simply increasing aspirin dosage may not be sufficient to overcome its limited systemic anti-inflammatory potential. It is also worth noting that higher doses also bring a higher risk of adverse effect risks such as bleeding in frail individuals, and any therapeutic effect at higher doses may be offset by this [ 28 ]. While our study shows neutral effect of aspirin on frailty, it does not preclude the potential for other anti-inflammatory agents to confer protective effects against frailty. Future trials investigating medications with more potent or targeted anti-inflammatory effects, still represent promising opportunities for frailty prevention and treatment.

A key strength of our study lies in it being a subgroup of a large, randomised trial and baseline characteristics were well balanced between the treatment arms. Furthermore, the large sample size drawn from the original ASPREE cohort provided substantial statistical power, ensuring data reliability within the studied demographic. Additionally, our analysis benefited from utilising two complementary frailty assessment models that were derived repeatedly during the follow-up period. Employing both frameworks allowed a comprehensive evaluation of frailty from different clinical perspectives, multidimensional cumulative deficits (FI) and physical phenotype-based assessments (FFP). Findings from both models consistently demonstrated aspirin’s null effects in frailty reversal, reinforcing the robustness of our conclusions. Finally, the use of linear-mixed effect model accounts for the dynamic nature of moving across different frailty levels, which overcomes the limitation of other models that only account for the first observed reversal.

Several limitations warrant consideration. Firstly, this study represents a secondary analysis of existing data from the ASPREE trial, originally designed to investigate aspirin’s role in prolonging disability-free survival rather than frailty specifically. As such, frailty assessment was not the primary or secondary endpoint of the original trial, potentially introducing measurement constraints or incomplete data capture related to frailty-specific criteria. Secondly, it remains uncertain whether higher-dose aspirin has greater physiological impact, modulating inflammation more effectively and thus influencing frailty trajectories differently. Thirdly, this study population predominantly consisted of White individuals. The generalisability of our findings to other racial/ethnic groups remains unclear. Last, while our linear-mixed model accounted for within-person variability, they don’t directly address measurement error caused by measurement inconsistency, which might lead to misclassification.

sections.conclusion: This study demonstrates that low-dose aspirin, compared to placebo, does not attenuate progression or improve frailty in prefrail or frail older adults. Future research may need to explore an integrated approach involving both pharmacological treatment and lifestyle modification for managing frailty.
